docs.title: Spring AI Session Extensions
docs.text:
Add-ons for the session support in Spring AI 2.1.

Spring AI 2.1 has the session itself: the event log, the stores, the ChatClient advisors, compaction and recall. This project adds features on top of it and changes nothing in it. It uses only the public extension points of the session: event types of its own, version-checked appends, and advisors around the session advisors.

Note

Experimental. The API can change between versions.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
Module Artifact Description Session Turn spring-ai-session-turn The TurnService: it starts, ends, interrupts, parks and resumes the turns of a session, and records each change as a TURN.* event in the session's log. It works with any Spring AI session store and does not depend on the ChatClient. Session Turn Advisor spring-ai-session-turn-advisor The ChatClient binding of the turn. The TurnStatusAdvisor runs every call as a turn, parks a turn whose tool call waits for a person's confirmation, and resumes it from the decisions. The TurnInterruptAdvisor stops the tool loop of an interrupted call. TurnAdvisors builds the whole advisor chain. Session Kafka spring-ai-session-kafka A SessionRepository that keeps sessions in Kafka, for teams that already run Kafka and want agent memory there, with no extra database. Each session has one owner that handles its calls one at a time, and the state is backed by compacted topics. It passes the Spring AI session repository contract tests. BOM spring-ai-session-extensions-bom Bill of Materials for the module versions.

Turn Status explains the turn service, and Turns in the ChatClient the ChatClient binding. Kafka Session Repository explains the Kafka store.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
The artifacts are on Maven Central. Import the BOM, so that the modules need no version:

<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springaicommunity</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-ai-session-extensions-bom</artifactId>
            <version>0.12.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

Then add the modules you use:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springaicommunity</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-ai-session-turn-advisor</artifactId>
</dependency>
To use Add It brings Turns in the ChatClient spring-ai-session-turn-advisor spring-ai-session-turn and Spring AI's spring-ai-session-advisor The turn service in a harness of your own spring-ai-session-turn Spring AI's spring-ai-session The Kafka session store spring-ai-session-kafka Spring AI's spring-ai-session, Spring for Apache Kafka and Kafka Streams

The BOM sets the versions of this project's modules only. Spring AI comes from its own BOM, spring-ai-bom, in version 2.1.0 or later.

docs.title: More stores
docs.text: Stores beyond the ones in Spring AI go into the session-repositories folder of the project. A store is built here first and moves into Spring AI when it is stable.

docs.title: Kafka Session Repository
docs.text:
spring-ai-session-kafka is a Kafka-based SessionRepository for the Spring AI session: sessions and their events are kept in Kafka. It works with DefaultSessionService and the session advisors unchanged, and passes the same contract suite as the JDBC store. It lets a team that already runs Kafka keep agent memory there, with no extra database.

Note

Experimental, tested on an embedded single broker. Production hardening, the Boot starter and multi-broker testing are still to come. The store and wire formats are not versioned yet, so data written by one 0.x release may not be readable by the next.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Under the hood, the store is a Kafka Streams topology that runs inside each application instance, built with Spring for Apache Kafka.

Every write rule of the session contract is per session: create-if-absent, the version check, idempotent append, delete. Calls are requests on a topic keyed by session id, so all calls for one session reach the one Streams task that owns its partition. That task handles its requests one at a time, which gives the guarantee a row lock gives JDBC.

 any instance         Kafka          partition owner
+------------+                     +---------------+
|Session-    |  1   +----------+   | 2 Streams task|
|Service     |----->| requests |-->|   checks and  |
|  |         |      +----------+   |   updates its |
|  v         |                     |   stores      |
|KafkaSession|      +----------+   | 3 changes go  |
|Repository  |      |changelogs|<--|   to changelog|
|            |  4   +----------+   | 4 reply, same |
|            |<-----| replies  |<--|   transaction |
+------------+      +----------+   +---------------+
  1. The repository sends the call with ReplyingKafkaTemplate to the session's partition.
  2. The owner task checks the rules and updates its RocksDB stores.
  3. Every store change also goes to a compacted changelog topic, which restores the store and erases deletes.
  4. The reply commits in the same exactly-once transaction as the changes; callers read replies read_committed.

Reads take the same path, so a read is ordered behind every earlier write to the session. Two calls span all sessions, listing a user's sessions and the expiry sweep: they go to every partition in parallel and the results are merged.

Every application instance is both a client and the owner of some partitions, assigned by the Streams group protocol. Which instance serves an HTTP request doesn't matter: the session's calls always reach its partition's owner, and no conversation state is kept on the caller.

docs.title: Stores
docs.text:
Store Key Value sessions session id the session, its event version, the next sequence number, the newest compaction boundary events length-prefixed session id + zero-padded sequence number the event, encoded with SessionEventCodec event-ids session id + event id the sequence number

A session's history is a prefixScan over events, in append order. An active-view read starts at the newest compaction boundary and adds the events it names, as JDBC does. Event ids are scoped to their session, which the contract allows.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
Add the dependency, with its version from the BOM:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springaicommunity</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-ai-session-kafka</artifactId>
</dependency>

KafkaSessionRepository repository = KafkaSessionRepository.builder()
    .bootstrapServers("broker:9092")
    .topicPrefix("my-app.ai-session")   // my-app.ai-session.requests / .replies
    .partitions(12)
    .build();
repository.start();                     // SmartLifecycle: a Spring context starts it

SessionService sessions = DefaultSessionService.builder()
    .sessionRepository(repository)
    .build();
Option Default Meaning bootstrapServers localhost:9092 Kafka brokers topicPrefix spring-ai-session Prefix of the requests and replies topics, and the Streams application id that names the consumer group and the changelogs; the same on every instance, and fixed once used partitions 12 Partitions of the topics, the most instances that share the work; fixed once created replicationFactor 3 Of every topic and changelog standbyReplicas 1 Warm copies of each store for fast takeover stateDirectory Streams default Where RocksDB keeps the stores operationTimeout 30 s How long a call waits for its reply contentRetention 1 day Retention of the requests and replies topics, and segment interval and compaction lag of every topic maxMessageBytes 8 MB Largest request, reply or changelog record kafkaProperties none Client properties such as security; the store's own settings win

isHealthy() turns false when this instance's Streams engine has stopped after a failure. Calls keep working, because its partitions move to the other instances, but the instance should be restarted.

docs.title: Guarantees
docs.text:
• Atomic state and reply. A caller never sees an answer whose store changes were rolled back.
  • Recovery. Stores restore from their changelogs: only the tail on the same disk, the whole compacted changelog on an empty one.
  • Erasure, eventually. A delete writes tombstones that compaction applies, and the requests and replies topics expire content by retention. Segment and compaction-lag settings use contentRetention, but erasure stays asynchronous: it waits for the segment to close, which needs a new record on the partition, and then for the log cleaner, which runs in the background.
  • Scale. Data and work are split by partition across instances.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Latency. Two Kafka hops and a transaction commit per call: about 2 ms per call and 5 ms per turn on an embedded broker; not measured on a real cluster.
  • Record size. A reply is about 2.4 times the text it carries, so a full-history read hits the 8 MB limit at roughly 3,500 events of 1 KB. Oversized requests and replies fail with a clear error and the store keeps serving.
  • Partition count. Fixed at creation; a mismatch stops startup, as does an existing topic or changelog with a smaller record limit or the wrong cleanup policy.
  • Replies go to every instance. Each instance reads all replies and keeps its own.
  • Search reads the whole log. searchEvents uses the default from SessionRepository: it reads the session's full history and filters it in the caller, so it has the same record size limit as a full-history read.
  • No JDBC transaction, like any non-JDBC store.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
The platform team sees the usual Kafka Streams surface:

  • a state directory per instance (a StatefulSet on Kubernetes, or a changelog restore on restart);
  • ACLs for the application id (the topic prefix), the changelog topics, the consumer group and the transactional ids;
  • rebalances on deploys, consumer lag and restore time, and RocksDB memory outside the heap.

The store's topic and record formats are internal; nothing else should write to them.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Suite What it covers KafkaSessionRepositoryTests The shared contract suite, on 4 partitions KafkaSessionRepositoryFailureTests An instance failing mid-request, malformed requests, client settings and topics that don't fit, a failed start KafkaSessionRepositoryInstancesTests Several instances: races, cross-partition calls, restarts, startup SessionMemoryAdvisorKafkaTests The session advisor's hooks across simulated tool rounds, with constructed model responses KafkaSessionRepositoryErasureTests A deleted session's text leaving every topic KafkaSessionRepositoryLimitsTests Record size limits

All run on an embedded single-node KRaft broker; no Docker is needed. They don't cover standby takeover, scale-out under load, broker failures, process kills, or production latency.

./mvnw verify -pl session-repositories/spring-ai-session-kafka -am

docs.title: Design notes
docs.text:
Rules the code keeps:

  • A record the producer refuses fails the task, and the request with it on every restart. Every request and reply is measured as Kafka will send it, key and headers included, and a write replies with no more than a flag, a count or a timestamp.
  • A request that can't be read is rejected while it is parsed, so the task skips it instead of failing on it.
  • The repository picks each session's partition itself, so producer partitioner settings can't split a session.
  • Creating a topic never changes an existing one, so startup checks the existing topics' partition count, record limit and cleanup policy.
  • A stopped Streams engine doesn't fail the instance's calls: the other instances still answer them.
  • The settings the guarantees rely on (exactly-once, failing on a processing error, compacted changelogs, committed restores) are set over the caller's kafkaProperties.

docs.title: Still open
docs.text:
• An index for listing a user's sessions (today each partition scans its sessions).
  • Bounded reads: a lastN window and the expiry sweep still read a partition's whole candidate set; both need large-data tests.
  • A shared RocksDB memory cap; today each store has default caches, which grow with partitions and standbys.
  • Smaller replies: the codec stores each message's text twice.
  • A native searchEvents, filtered by the partition owner instead of the caller.
  • A versioning policy and compatibility fixtures for the store and wire formats.
  • Standby takeover, scale-out under load, and a multi-broker Testcontainers run.
  • Taking the application's Kafka factories, and a Boot starter with a health indicator on isHealthy().

docs.title: Turns in the ChatClient
docs.text: spring-ai-session-turn-advisor runs every ChatClient call as a turn, with the turn service. It starts the turn before the call and ends it after. When the tool loop pauses on a tool call that needs a confirmation, it parks the turn instead of ending it. A later call with the person's decisions resumes it, on any instance.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
Add the dependency, with its version from the BOM:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springaicommunity</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-ai-session-turn-advisor</artifactId>
</dependency>

It brings the turn service and the Spring AI session advisors.

TurnAdvisors builds the advisor chain: the Spring AI session advisors, and the two advisors of this module around them.

ChatClient chatClient = ChatClient.builder(chatModel)
    .defaultAdvisors(TurnAdvisors.builder(sessionService).build())
    .defaultTools(tools)
    .build();

A call names its session, as with the Spring AI session advisors. When it pauses on a tool call, the response names the calls that await a decision, and the session is parked:

ChatResponse response = chatClient.prompt()
    .user("Book flight VX205")
    .advisors(SessionAdvisors.session(sessionId))
    .call()
    .chatResponse();

List<String> awaiting = ToolCallDecisions.awaitingDecision(response);   // ["c1"]; empty when the call did not pause

Later, on any instance, a call with the person's decisions and no user message resumes it:

ToolCallDecisions decisions = ToolCallDecisions.of(ToolCallDecision.allow("c1"));

chatClient.prompt()
    .advisors(TurnStatusAdvisor.decisions(sessionId, decisions))
    .call()
    .content();

TurnStatusAdvisor.decisions sets the session id and the decisions in the advisor context. The request must carry the tools of the allowed calls. Tools set with defaultTools are on every request. Tools passed to a single call must be passed again with the decisions.

The module uses these context keys:

Context key Value session_tool_call_decisions (TOOL_CALL_DECISIONS_CONTEXT_KEY) The ToolCallDecisions that answer the parked tool calls. session_run_id (RUN_ID_CONTEXT_KEY) The run id of the turn. TurnStatusAdvisor.runId(runId) sets it; the advisor sets it on the response. See the run id. session_turn_id (TURN_ID_CONTEXT_KEY) The id of the turn. The advisor sets it on the request it forwards, for the interrupt check. You do not set it.

docs.title: The run id
docs.text:
Each call runs as a turn under a run id. The advisor takes it from the request context under session_run_id, or generates one. It puts the run id into the context of the request it forwards and of the response.

TurnStatusAdvisor.runId(runId) sets the run id for a call that starts a turn and for one that resumes it:

chatClient.prompt()
    .user("Book flight VX205")
    .advisors(SessionAdvisors.session(sessionId))
    .advisors(TurnStatusAdvisor.runId("run-1"))
    .call()
    .content();

A resume without a run id runs under a new one. To keep the run id of the paused call, pass it with the decisions. The run id is stored in the session's log, so the status of a parked session still has it, on any instance and after a restart:

TurnService turns = new TurnService(sessionService);
String runId = turns.status(sessionId).runId();   // the run id of the parked turn

chatClient.prompt()
    .advisors(TurnStatusAdvisor.decisions(sessionId, decisions))
    .advisors(TurnStatusAdvisor.runId(runId))
    .call()
    .content();

The paused response has the same run id in its context, under TurnStatusAdvisor.RUN_ID_CONTEXT_KEY, for a caller that still holds it.

docs.title: It wraps the Spring AI advisors
docs.text:
Spring AI 2.1 already has session advisors for the ChatClient. This module does not replace them. It adds one advisor in front of them and one behind them, and leaves them as they are.

Turns in the ChatClient The advisor chain of a ChatClient with the TurnStatusAdvisor of this project in front of the Spring AI session advisors and its TurnInterruptAdvisor behind them. TurnStatusAdvisor runs once per call: it starts, parks, resumes and ends the turn through the TurnService, which writes TURN events through the SessionService. SessionTurnAdvisor runs once per call: it creates the session and compacts it. ToolCallingAdvisor runs the loop and the tools through the ToolCallingManager, and pauses on a tool call that needs a confirmation; for each tool round the rest of the chain runs again. SessionMemoryAdvisor stores the messages and builds the prompt on every round. TurnInterruptAdvisor of this project checks on every round that the turn still runs, and stops the loop after an interrupt. ChatModelCallAdvisor, the last advisor, calls the chat model. The Spring AI advisors are unchanged. Turns in the ChatClient The advisor chain of a ChatClient advisors, by order (HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + n) TurnStatusAdvisoronce per call: starts, parks, resumes, ends the turn+100 SessionTurnAdvisoronce per call: creates the session, compacts+200 ToolCallingAdvisorthe loop: runs tools, pauses on a confirmation+300 SessionMemoryAdvisorevery round: stores the messages, builds the prompt+1000 TurnInterruptAdvisorevery round: stops the loop after an interrupt+1100 ChatModelCallAdvisorcalls the modellast for each tool round what the chain calls TurnServiceTURN.STATUS, QUESTION, ANSWER events SessionServicethe event log, kept in a session store ToolCallingManager & Toolssome need a person's confirmation Spring AI Session Extensions Spring AI 2.1, unchanged ChatModel

A lower order runs further out. The ToolCallingAdvisor runs the advisors after it again for each tool round, so the SessionMemoryAdvisor stores every round. The TurnInterruptAdvisor runs on every round too, before the model is called. The TurnStatusAdvisor and the SessionTurnAdvisor run once per call. So the TurnStatusAdvisor sees the whole call, and it sees the response after the Spring AI advisors stored it.

The TurnStatusAdvisor does three things the Spring AI advisors do not:

  • It records the turn. start before the call, end after, park when the response is a paused reply.
  • It resumes a parked turn from decisions. The request carries the person's decisions and no user message.
  • It closes a pause when new text arrives. See new text on a parked session.

docs.title: A paused tool call and its resume
docs.text:
Two calls. The first one pauses on a tool that needs a confirmation. The second one carries the decisions and finishes the turn.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Application
    participant T as TurnStatusAdvisor
    participant TS as TurnService
    participant S as Spring AI advisors<br/>(turn, tool loop, memory)
    participant M as Model

    A->>T: prompt "Book flight VX205"
    T->>TS: start(sessionId, runId)
    T->>S: request
    S->>M: prompt with the stored history
    M-->>S: reply: call bookFlight
    Note over S: memory stores the reply,<br/>tool loop pauses: bookFlight needs a confirmation
    S-->>T: paused reply
    T->>TS: park(sessionId, turn, ToolConfirmationQuestion)
    T-->>A: paused reply, awaiting a decision

    Note over A: the person decides, later,<br/>maybe on another instance

    A->>T: prompt with decisions, no user message
    T->>TS: resume(sessionId, runId, decisions)
    T->>T: run the allowed calls<br/>through the ToolCallingManager
    T->>T: store the results after the reply
    T->>S: request without messages
    S->>M: prompt: the turn so far and the results
    M-->>S: "Your flight is booked."
    S-->>T: answer
    T->>TS: end(sessionId, turn, END_TURN)
    T-->>A: answer

On the resume, the TurnStatusAdvisor stores the tool results right after the paused reply, and forwards the request without messages. Spring AI's turn advisor sees that the open calls have results and leaves them alone. Spring AI's memory advisor builds the prompt from the log, so the model gets the whole turn. When an allowed call's tool returns directly, its result is the answer, and the model is not called.

docs.title: Asking the person
docs.text:
The paused response names the calls that await a decision. An application that still holds it can ask the person at once. Another instance, or the same one after a restart, reads the question from the session's log instead:

TurnService turns = new TurnService(sessionService);

SessionEvent pending = turns.pendingQuestion(sessionId);   // null when the session waits on nothing
ToolConfirmationQuestion question = ToolConfirmationQuestion.from(pending);

for (ToolConfirmationQuestion.ToolCall call : question.toolCalls()) {
    // call.name() and call.arguments() are what to show the person
    // call.awaitingDecision() tells whether the person must decide on it
}

The answer has one decision for each call, named by call.key():

List<ToolCallDecision> decisions = question.toolCalls().stream()
    .map(call -> !call.awaitingDecision() || approved(call)
            ? ToolCallDecision.allow(call.key())
            : ToolCallDecision.deny(call.key(), "The user declined the booking."))
    .toList();

chatClient.prompt()
    .advisors(TurnStatusAdvisor.decisions(sessionId, new ToolCallDecisions(decisions)))
    .call()
    .content();

approved stands for what the person chose. A call that does not await a decision needs no confirmation, so the example allows it.

ToolConfirmationQuestion.from refuses a question of another kind. When your harness also parks on questions of its own, read the kind first, with Question.from(pending).kind().

docs.title: When the tools run
docs.text:
A paused reply can hold several tool calls, and only some of them may need a confirmation.

  • No call of a paused reply runs before the resume. Spring AI checks the whole reply before it runs any call. When one call needs a confirmation, none runs, also not the calls that need none.
  • The decisions cover every call of the reply. A call that needs no confirmation still needs a decision, because it has not run yet.
  • A denied call does not run. Its result is the message of the denial, and the model reads it.
  • An allowed call runs once, on the resume. The advisor records the answer first, then runs the calls, then stores the results. A second call with the same decisions is refused, because the question already has its answer.
  • The tool calls of earlier rounds already ran. A turn can run several tool rounds before one of them pauses. Their results are in the log, and the resume does not touch them.

Decisions name the calls by key, not the question they answer. When the turn has parked again on a new question, decisions made for the old one are refused because their keys do not match the new reply. A model that sends no tool call ids gets position keys (#0, #1), and there old decisions can match the calls of the new question.

docs.title: When a resume fails
docs.text:
The answer is recorded before the tools run. So an allowed call runs at most once, and a failure never runs it a second time.

  • The run of the allowed calls fails. The turn ends with ERROR. Every call of the reply gets the result "No result was recorded for this tool call.", so the log keeps no call without a result.
  • The instance dies during the resume. The turn stays RUNNING, and another resume is refused. A tool may have run without its result in the log. Free the session with TurnService.interrupt. On the next call, Spring AI's turn advisor gives the calls without a result the same "No result was recorded" result.

docs.title: What the TurnStatusAdvisor decides on each call
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A([A call arrives]) --> R{Does another turn run?}
    R -- yes --> X([Refuse with TurnInProgressException])
    R -- no --> B{Is the session parked?}
    B -- no --> C[start the turn]
    B -- yes --> D{Does the request carry decisions?}
    D -- yes --> E[resume with the decisions,<br/>run the allowed calls,<br/>store the results]
    D -- no --> F[resume with every call denied,<br/>store the denials,<br/>send the text on]
    C --> G[Forward to the Spring AI advisors]
    E --> G
    F --> G
    G --> H{Is the response a paused reply?}
    H -- yes --> I([park the turn on the question])
    H -- no --> J{Did the call fail?}
    J -- no --> K([end with END_TURN])
    J -- yes --> L([end with ERROR])

docs.title: Refused requests
docs.text:
These requests are refused, and nothing is written:

Request Exception Any call while another turn runs on the session TurnInProgressException Decisions on a session that is not parked, or that does not exist IllegalStateException Decisions on a session parked on a question of another kind, or whose paused reply is no longer its newest message IllegalStateException Decisions for a question another caller answered first IllegalStateException, or TurnInProgressException while that caller's turn runs Decisions together with a user message IllegalArgumentException Decisions that miss a call of the paused reply, or name a call it does not have IllegalArgumentException An allowed call whose tool the request does not carry IllegalArgumentException

An IllegalArgumentException means the request is wrong. An IllegalStateException means the session is not in a state for it.

docs.title: New text on a parked session
docs.text:
New text always moves a parked session on. The person did not decide, so the advisor closes the question before the text goes on:

  • The session waits on the tool confirmation of its newest reply. The advisor stores a denial for each open tool call, with the text of TurnStatusAdvisor.ABANDONED_DENY_MESSAGE. The log then says the calls were denied, not that they have no result.
  • The session waits on a question of another kind, or the log changed since it parked. The question gets an empty answer, and no tool runs.

docs.title: Interrupting a running call
docs.text:
TurnService.interrupt(sessionId, reason) ends the running turn at once, from a stop button or another instance. The session is then free for the next turn.

The interrupted call must stop too. Otherwise its tool loop goes on, and its messages land in between those of the next turn. The TurnInterruptAdvisor stops it. Before each model round it checks that the call's turn still runs, and throws TurnInterruptedException when it does not. The rounds that already ran stay in the log, with their tool results.

try {
    chatClient.prompt().user("...").advisors(SessionAdvisors.session(sessionId)).call().content();
}
catch (TurnInterruptedException ex) {
    // ex.getStatus().stopReason() is INTERRUPTED
}

With stream() the exception is the error signal of the Flux. The failed call does not change the status: it stays as the interrupt left it. The check is one indexed read per model round. A tool that already runs is not stopped: the loop stops before the next model round. TurnAdvisors adds the advisor by default, and interruptible(false) leaves it out.

docs.title: Configuring the advisors
docs.text:
TurnAdvisors builds the whole chain at the right orders. The settings the advisors share are set once, so they cannot differ.

ChatClient chatClient = ChatClient.builder(chatModel)
    .defaultAdvisors(TurnAdvisors.builder(sessionService)
        .sessionIdInToolContext(true)
        .sessionAdvisors(session -> session.compaction(trigger, strategy))
        .build())
    .build();
Setting What it does sessionIdInToolContext(true) Tools get the session id in their tool context. It applies to the calls of the loop and to the allowed calls of a resume alike. toolCallingManager(manager) The manager that runs the allowed calls of a resume. Use the one the ChatClient's tool-calling advisor uses. scheduler(scheduler) The scheduler for the session calls of a streamed call, for every advisor. interruptible(false) Leaves the TurnInterruptAdvisor out. sessionAdvisors(session -> ...) The settings of the Spring AI session advisors, compaction for example.

You can also build the three parts yourself, with TurnStatusAdvisor.builder, SessionAdvisors.builder and TurnInterruptAdvisor.builder.

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text: A streamed call works the same way. A streamed pause ends on a last chunk that names the calls awaiting a decision, and the advisor parks the turn when the stream completes. A stream that fails ends the turn with ERROR. A stream the client cancels ends it with CANCELLED, also when the client leaves while the turn is still starting. A client that cancels after the last chunk does not change the outcome: the turn is parked or ended as the stream finished. The session calls run on a scheduler, never on the model's thread, and a cancel never interrupts them.

docs.title: Turn Status
docs.text:
A turn is one piece of work a harness does on a session: from a user's message to the model's last answer, with every tool call in between. spring-ai-session-turn records in the session's log whether a turn runs, under which run id, and why the last one ended.

This solves three problems that a plain conversation log has:

  • Two harnesses can run one session at the same time. Two instances, or two browser tabs, append their messages in between each other's. With a turn status, the second one is refused.
  • A running turn cannot be stopped from elsewhere. A stop button on another instance has nothing to write to. With a turn status, it records an interrupt that the running harness reads.
  • A turn that waits for a person is lost on a restart. A tool call that needs a confirmation pauses the turn, and the pause lives only in memory. With a turn status, the question is in the log, and any instance can resume the turn with the answer.

The module works with any Spring AI session store, because it uses only what every store has: events of its own type, a read by type, and a version-checked append.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
Add the dependency, with its version from the BOM:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springaicommunity</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-ai-session-turn</artifactId>
</dependency>

Create the turn service on a Spring AI SessionService, and run each turn between start and end:

TurnService turns = new TurnService(sessionService);

TurnStatus turn;
try {
    turn = turns.start(sessionId, runId);
}
catch (TurnInProgressException ex) {
    return busy(ex.getRunId());                     // another turn runs: refuse, a 409 for example
}
catch (TurnParkedException ex) {
    return ask(turns.pendingQuestion(sessionId));   // the session waits for an answer
}

try {
    // run the turn: call the model, run tools, append messages
    turns.end(sessionId, turn, StopReason.END_TURN);
}
catch (RuntimeException ex) {
    turns.end(sessionId, turn, StopReason.ERROR);
    throw ex;
}

busy and ask stand for what your application does. A refused start writes nothing and owns no turn. That is why it stays outside the second try: there is no turn to end.

From anywhere else, a UI or another instance:

turns.status(sessionId);                          // RUNNING under run-7, or IDLE with a stop reason
turns.interrupt(sessionId, "user pressed stop");  // ends the running turn

TurnService keeps no state. It reads and writes through the SessionService, so you can create one per call or keep one.

docs.title: What the log holds
docs.text:
Every change is an event in the session's log.

Event type Written when Payload TURN.STATUS A turn starts, ends, parks or resumes status, runId, stopReason TURN.INTERRUPT Someone asks the running turn to stop reason TURN.QUESTION A turn stops to wait for an answer kind, value TURN.ANSWER The answer arrives and the turn goes on questionEventId, value

None of these events carries a message. The session's active view holds message events only, so these events never reach a prompt, and a compaction never covers them. They stay in the log as the record of the session's turns.

The status of a session is its newest TURN.STATUS event. A session without one is IDLE. There is no status column and no second store: the log is the only source.

docs.title: Status and stop reasons
docs.text:
A session is RUNNING while a turn runs, and IDLE otherwise. An idle session tells why its last turn ended:

Stop reason Meaning END_TURN The turn ran to its end. ERROR The turn failed. INTERRUPTED Someone called interrupt. A TURN.INTERRUPT event sits right before it. CANCELLED The client stopped listening, a cancelled stream for example. Nobody asked the session to stop, so there is no TURN.INTERRUPT event. REQUIRES_ACTION The turn is parked on a question and waits for an answer.

docs.title: What each method does in each state
docs.text:
For the methods of the turn service, a session is in one of three states:

  • Idle. No turn runs and no question is open. The status is IDLE with any stop reason but REQUIRES_ACTION, or the session has no status yet.
  • Running. A turn runs. The status is RUNNING.
  • Parked. A turn stopped on a question and waits for the answer. The status is IDLE with REQUIRES_ACTION. See a turn that waits for a person.
stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR
    [*] --> Idle
    Idle --> Running : start
    Running --> Idle : end, interrupt
    Running --> Parked : park
    Parked --> Running : resume
Method Idle Running Parked start Starts a turn. Throws TurnInProgressException. Throws TurnParkedException. end Writes nothing. Ends the turn, when it is the caller's. Writes nothing. park Writes nothing. Parks the turn, when it is the caller's. Writes nothing. interrupt Records the request. Records the request and ends the turn with INTERRUPTED. Records the request. The question stays open. resume Throws IllegalStateException. Throws TurnInProgressException. Records the answer and runs the turn again.

status and pendingQuestion only read.

Two rules of the parked state are easy to miss:

  • start refuses a parked session. A new turn would leave the question open. Resume the session instead.
  • interrupt does not close a question. A parked session has no turn to stop, so the session stays parked. To close the question, resume with an answer that says the person moved on.

docs.title: The run id
docs.text:
Every turn runs under a run id. The run id names the harness run that owns the turn: a request, a job, an agent run. The session does not interpret it.

  • start and resume take a run id. When you pass null, they generate a random UUID. The returned status carries the run id either way.
  • end and park take the turn, not the run id. The turn is the status that start or resume returned. A run id may repeat, so only that status tells one turn from a later one under the same run id.
  • interrupt takes no run id. It ends whatever turn runs, so a stop button does not need to know the owner.
  • A refused start names the owner. TurnInProgressException.getRunId() returns the run id of the turn that runs.
  • An idle session keeps the run id of its last turn, next to the stop reason.

A resume does not have to use the run id of the turn that parked. The turn often resumes on another instance, or hours later, under a run of its own. Pass the old run id to keep one run id across the pause, or pass null for a new one.

TurnStatus parked = turns.park(sessionId, turn, question);           // IDLE, run-1, REQUIRES_ACTION

turns.resume(sessionId, parked.runId(), answer);                     // RUNNING under run-1 again
turns.resume(sessionId, null, answer);                               // or RUNNING under a new run id

docs.title: How a change is written
docs.text:
Every method that changes the status follows the same steps. It reads the log's version, then the current status, and decides. Then it appends its events with the version it read. If another writer appended in between, the store refuses the append, and the method reads again and decides again. After five refused attempts it gives up with an IllegalStateException.

This is what makes two concurrent starts safe: both read the same version, both try to append, and the store accepts exactly one.

The activity of start:

flowchart TD
    A([start sessionId, runId]) --> B[Read the log's version]
    B --> C[Read the newest TURN.STATUS event]
    C --> D{Does a turn run?}
    D -- yes --> E([Throw TurnInProgressException<br/>with the running run id])
    D -- no --> F{Is the session parked?}
    F -- yes --> G([Throw TurnParkedException])
    F -- no --> H[Append TURN.STATUS RUNNING<br/>against the version read]
    H --> I{Did the store accept it?}
    I -- yes --> J([Return RUNNING under the run id])
    I -- no --> K{Fifth attempt?}
    K -- no --> B
    K -- yes --> L([Throw IllegalStateException])

end, interrupt, park and resume follow the same loop with their own decision:

  • end writes only while the caller's turn runs. Otherwise it writes nothing and returns the status as it stands. So a harness ends only its own turn: a late end never ends a later turn, and an interrupt that landed first stands.
  • interrupt writes the TURN.INTERRUPT event and, when a turn runs, the TURN.STATUS event that ends it, in one append.
  • park and resume are described below.

docs.title: The types
docs.text:
classDiagram
    direction LR
    class TurnService {
        +TurnService(SessionService)
        +status(sessionId) TurnStatus
        +start(sessionId, runId) TurnStatus
        +end(sessionId, turn, StopReason) TurnStatus
        +interrupt(sessionId, reason) TurnStatus
        +park(sessionId, turn, Question) TurnStatus

    class TurnStatus {

    }
    class SessionStatus {
        <<enumeration>>
        IDLE
        RUNNING
    }
    class StopReason {
        <<enumeration>>
        END_TURN

    class Question {

    TurnService --> SessionService : reads and writes through
    TurnService ..> TurnStatus : returns
    TurnService ..> Question : parks on
    TurnStatus --> SessionStatus
    TurnStatus --> StopReason
    Answer ..> Question : answers
    ToolConfirmationQuestion ..> Question : converts to

SessionService is Spring AI's interface. TurnEventTypes holds the four event types, and SessionStatusEvents and QuestionEvents build and read the events. The diagram leaves those helpers out.

docs.title: A turn that waits for a person
docs.text:
A turn can stop to ask a person something and go on later with the answer, on any instance, after any delay. The built-in kind of question is a tool confirmation: a tool call that needs a person's decision. A harness can also park on a question of its own kind.

  • park writes a TURN.QUESTION event and a TURN.STATUS event IDLE with REQUIRES_ACTION, in one append. The session is then parked. It holds no turn while the person thinks.
  • pendingQuestion returns the open question: the newest TURN.QUESTION event when no TURN.ANSWER follows it.
  • resume writes a TURN.ANSWER event that points at the question, and a TURN.STATUS event RUNNING, in one append. Only a parked session resumes, so the same answer sent twice resumes once.
  • resume with a question id refuses when that question already has an answer. Pass the id of the question you read with pendingQuestion. Two callers that read the same question then cannot both resume: the second one fails, even when the turn has parked again on a new question in between.

ToolConfirmationQuestion is the shape of a tool confirmation. It holds the event id of the stored reply and the reply's tool calls, each marked whether it waits for a decision. The answer is Spring AI's ToolCallDecisions.

A harness parks a turn and a UI resumes it:

sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Harness
    participant U as UI
    participant T as TurnService
    participant S as SessionService

    H->>T: start(sessionId, "run-1")
    T->>S: getEventVersion, newest TURN.STATUS
    T->>S: appendEvents [TURN.STATUS RUNNING]
    Note over H: the model asks for a tool<br/>that needs a confirmation
    H->>T: park(sessionId, turn, question)
    T->>S: appendEvents [TURN.QUESTION,<br/>TURN.STATUS IDLE REQUIRES_ACTION]
    Note over H,S: the harness may stop here, even restart
    U->>T: pendingQuestion(sessionId)
    T->>S: newest TURN.QUESTION or TURN.ANSWER
    T-->>U: the question
    U->>T: resume(sessionId, "run-2", decisions)
    T->>S: appendEvents [TURN.ANSWER,<br/>TURN.STATUS RUNNING]
    Note over U,S: the harness runs the allowed tools<br/>and the turn goes on

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text:
• No guard on the log. An append never needs a running turn. A harness that does not call start still appends its messages, also while another turn runs. So the turn status protects a session only when every harness that writes to it runs its turns through the turn service.
  • No lease. A turn whose harness died stays RUNNING until someone calls interrupt, which ends it. A later version can add a lease that lets the next start take over a turn that ran too long.
  • One answer per question. The answer decides every tool call of the question at once. An application that collects decisions one by one holds them until it has all.
  • No stop by itself. An interrupt changes the status. The harness that runs the turn learns of it only when it reads the status, between two model calls for example. Check with turns.status(sessionId).stillRuns(turn). The ChatClient binding does this check for you.
  • No transaction around it. Run the turn service outside a surrounding transaction. Inside one with repeatable read isolation, the version read does not see what another writer committed, and every attempt fails.
